---
title: "About Quarto 2"
description: "Why Quarto 2 exists, what it aims to do, and how it relates to Quarto 1 and Pandoc."
---

Quarto 2 is a full rewrite of the Quarto CLI in Rust, developed in the open at [quarto-dev/q2](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2) under the MIT license, like Quarto 1. It is experimental: it works today for many documents and websites, but it is not yet a replacement for Quarto 1.

This page collects what the Quarto team has said publicly about why Quarto 2 exists and the principles behind it. Each section links to the original statement.

## Why a rewrite?

Quarto 1 combines several tools (Deno and TypeScript, Pandoc, Lua filters, engines) that each work well, but some problems sit in how they fit together. In the [announcement](https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-04-06_whats-next-quarto-2/) the team explains that, given the team's size, fixing these one at a time no longer paid off:

> There are some fundamental pain points in Quarto 1 that can't be solved incrementally.

A frequently requested example is mapping rendered output back to the exact place in the `.qmd` source it came from. Doing this properly [needs a new Markdown parser, a new Lua filter system, source-aware data types and a matching YAML parser](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/discussions/14873#discussioncomment-18368861). That is not a feature to add to Quarto 1; it is the foundation of Quarto 2.

## Goals

The [announcement](https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-04-06_whats-next-quarto-2/) names these goals:

- **Diagnostics throughout the pipeline.** A new Markdown parser lets editors and the command line report syntax errors, broken links and invalid options with precise locations, not only for YAML.
- **Performance.** The performance-critical parts are one Rust code base. In early experiments Quarto 2 was [about 50 times faster than Quarto 1](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/issues/6771#issuecomment-4563806955), and it is [small enough to run inside a browser tab](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-hub).
- **Collaboration.** A built-in collaborative editor, [Quarto Hub](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-hub), built on the open-source [Automerge](https://automerge.org) library.
- **Bidirectional editing.** People using a visual editor and people editing the source can work on the same document: a small change in one should be a small change in the `.qmd` file.
- **Compatibility.** Quarto 2 aims to be backwards compatible with Quarto 1 projects, extensions and Pandoc output formats. Early on there will be gaps, so it is initially a better fit for new projects.

## Design principles

### Syntax errors instead of guesses

Most Markdown parsers accept any input and quietly guess what incomplete markup meant. Quarto 2 reports an error instead. The [parsing post](https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-05-07_quarto-2-parsing/) explains why the team rejects the CommonMark principle that every input is a valid document, and the [Markdown migration guide](guides/authoring/migrating-markdown.qmd) lists each case with its fix:

> Pandoc guesses what you meant when markup is incomplete, and q2 reports an error instead.

Every diagnostic has a code and its own page in the [error reference](errors/index.qmd).

### Source locations everywhere

Quarto 2 keeps track of where every piece of a document came from, through parsing, configuration merging, filters and output. This is what makes precise error messages, editor features and collaborative editing possible ([parsing post](https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-05-07_quarto-2-parsing/)).

### Explicit instead of inferred

Where Quarto 1 inferred behavior from the presence of a file or from context, Quarto 2 tends to ask for an explicit declaration, so that, for example, [a file's presence never silently changes how a project renders](guides/authoring/brand.qmd).

### A stable syntax for the long term

The team wants Quarto to have "a useful lifespan of at least 10 to 20 years" ([parsing post](https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-05-07_quarto-2-parsing/)). Owning the parser lets the syntax be specified and held stable. That syntax stays Markdown: "Quarto's plain-text document format is going to be (some close variant of) Markdown for the lifetime of the project" ([discussion](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/discussions/14681#discussioncomment-17626734)).

### Meet communities where they are

Quarto keeps using the tools each community already relies on, such as Jupyter for Python and knitr for R, rather than introducing a new execution model ([discussion](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/discussions/15200#discussioncomment-19247156)).

## Relationship to Quarto 1

Quarto 1 continues to be developed and maintained in parallel until Quarto 2 can replace it ([announcement](https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-04-06_whats-next-quarto-2/)). Quarto 2 is not perfectly backwards compatible: a few Markdown constructs are deliberately unsupported (see the [migration guide](guides/authoring/migrating-markdown.qmd)), and some Quarto 1 features are not ported yet. To ease the move, Quarto 1 is starting to accept Quarto 2 syntax, for example the [definition-list syntax in Quarto 1.11](https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-11-02_quarto-1-11/).

## Relationship to Pandoc

Quarto 2 reads Markdown with its own parser instead of Pandoc's, and it supports only its own Markdown dialect, which stays close to Pandoc Markdown. The parser produces the same kind of document tree as Pandoc, and its JSON form is Pandoc-compatible, so filters written against Pandoc's document model still apply. For HTML, Quarto 2 writes the output itself. For other formats, such as Word, PowerPoint, EPUB and Typst, it hands the document to [Pandoc](https://pandoc.org) ([other output formats](guides/formats/pandoc/index.qmd)).

The [parsing post](https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-05-07_quarto-2-parsing/) explains the reasons for the new parser: actionable syntax errors, source locations that survive the whole pipeline, and control over syntax stability.

## Collaboration and Quarto Hub

[Quarto Hub](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-hub) is a collaborative editor that renders the document as you type, with the same `.qmd` files underneath. It runs Quarto 2 in the browser and syncs changes with Automerge. The editor and the sync protocol are open source; the hosted instance at [quarto-hub.com](https://quarto-hub.com) is a live demo. Carlos Scheidegger, who leads Quarto 2, has said that "a solid version of Quarto 2's collaborative writer will forever be open source" ([Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/rstats/comments/1v4pqz9/shinyappsio_rpubs_quarto_pub_are_migrating_to/)).

## Status and how to take part

Quarto 2 is experimental and changes quickly. The team is [not yet taking feature requests](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/discussions/258), because much of the architecture and design is still in flux. Questions, suggestions and bug reports are welcome in the [q2 discussions](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/discussions) and [issues](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/issues).
